content.text: Strategic planning and continuous school improvement are the foundation of educational excellence at Eduversal Partner Schools. This section sets out the framework Principals use to lead their schools. With it, Principals set strategic direction, track progress toward goals and keep improvement going over time. This improvement supports our mission: to deliver world-class Cambridge education while honoring Indonesian values and identity. Good strategic planning helps Principals to:

items: Translate Vision into Action: Turn the school's mission and its Schoolwide Learner Outcomes into measurable goals and operational priorities. The outcomes are Academic Excellence, Communication, Global Competence, Ethical Leadership, Innovation and Wellbeing. These goals and priorities guide daily decisions at all levels of the organization.

Align Stakeholder Efforts: Bring the Yayasan Foundation, the Eduversal management team, teaching staff, parents and students together around shared priorities. Everyone then works toward common objectives, instead of on separate, disconnected initiatives.

Drive Continuous Improvement: Set up regular cycles of planning, implementation, monitoring and reflection. These cycles make improvement part of the school's culture, not something done now and then or as a reaction to problems.

Demonstrate Accountability: Give clear evidence of progress to several groups of stakeholders. Parents want a return on their investment. The Yayasan takes care of its resources. Eduversal leadership monitors network quality. Accreditation bodies evaluate how effective the institution is.

Optimize Resource Allocation: Make informed decisions about budget, staffing, facilities and time. Base them on strategic priorities, not on past habits or competing pressures. This is especially important in our resource-conscious Indonesian context.

Prepare for Accreditation: Build the culture of evidence-based reflection and documentation required for CIS/WASC accreditation. At the same time, meet Indonesian regulatory requirements for school development planning (RKS/RKAS).

content.text: Strategic planning at Eduversal Partner Schools works within a unique governance context (see Section 1: Governance Charter). The Principal is the instructional and operational leader. The Principal works closely with the General Manager (also known as Foundation Representative, Eduversal's on-site representative). The Principal is accountable to both the local Yayasan Foundation and Eduversal's Board of Trustees. This dual accountability requires strategic plans that do two things. They honor local context and ownership. They also stay aligned with network-wide standards and the Cambridge curriculum framework.

content.title: Quality Management System (QMS)
content.text:
Eduversal's QMS keeps quality consistent across all Partner Schools through:

**EduNav:** An integrated school management platform (by PT. Global Zerone Digital). It gives real-time dashboards, KPI tracking and evidence repositories. These move strategic planning from a document-based practice to a data-driven one.

**EASE (Eduversal Analytical & Skills Evaluation):** Standardized assessments across the three EASE programs: EASE Growth and EASE Assessment for students, and EASE Academic for teachers. The Eduversal Academic Board's Subject Specialist team organizes them, and Latihan.id delivers them. Each program runs on its own schedule. Each gives useful data for improving teaching.

**DTP (Development of Teaching Proficiency):** A professional development program (by PT. Edukasi Universal Indonesia / Educamp). It builds teacher capacity through training, coaching and classroom support linked to school improvement priorities.

**Appraisal Program:** A dual evaluation system that includes:

**School Appraisal:** Annual institutional evaluation across 5 domains by the QMS Team

**Teacher Appraisal:** Ongoing lesson observations and assessment of teaching quality
Compliance and Regulatory Frameworks

steps: Indonesian RKS/RKAS: Compliance with PP No. 57/2021 Pasal 28 requirements for two plans submitted to local education authorities. The first is the 4-year medium-term school development plan (Rencana Kerja Sekolah). The second is the annual activity and budget plans (Rencana Kegiatan dan Anggaran Sekolah).
CIS/WASC Standards: Alignment with international accreditation standards and ongoing preparation for self-study processes.
Cambridge Centre Requirements: Ongoing compliance with Cambridge International examination center standards.

EASE Week: One of four weeks in the school year, two per semester, set aside for EASE testing. Weeks 1 and 3 fall in the middle of the semester. They carry the EASE Growth sitting, and normal lessons continue. Weeks 2 and 4 fall at the end of the semester. They carry the Synchronized Test, and normal lessons stop for the week

Every Eduversal Partner School keeps a full 3-5 year Strategic Plan. The plan sets out the school's vision for development and the roadmap to achieve its mission. This medium-term plan gives stability and direction. It still allows yearly adjustments when new needs or changed circumstances appear.
The Multi-Year Strategic Plan is the school's main vision document. It covers:
content.title: 4.2.1 Multi-Year Strategic Plan (3-5 Years)

items: Educational Direction: How the school will develop its curriculum, teaching methods and assessment practices. The aim is to achieve the six Schoolwide Learner Outcomes (Academic Excellence, Communication, Global Competence, Ethical Leadership, Innovation, and Wellbeing) and Indonesian character competencies.
Organizational Development: How governance structures, leadership capacity, staffing models and professional learning systems need to develop to support educational goals.
Enrollment and Financial Sustainability: Expected growth in student numbers, tuition strategy, new sources of revenue, and investment priorities that fit the school's market position.
Facilities and Resources: Capital improvements, technology infrastructure, better learning environments, and the resources needed to support 21st-century learning.

Accreditation and Compliance: The pathway toward CIS/WASC accreditation and keeping Cambridge Centre status. It also covers ongoing compliance with Indonesian regulatory requirements (see Section 2: Indonesian Compliance and Section 3: Cambridge Centre Compliance).

Community and Partnerships: Strategies to strengthen parent engagement, develop alumni networks and build local community relationships. They also position the school within Indonesia's competitive international education market.

content.text: The Principal leads the development of the Strategic Plan together with the General Manager. The process is collaborative and gathers input from many stakeholders:

steps: Environmental Scanning (Months 1-2 of planning cycle): Use a SWOT analysis to study the internal and external factors that affect the school. Review enrollment trends, parent satisfaction data, academic results, staff retention patterns, competitor positioning, regulatory changes and community demographics. The Appraisal evaluation gives a full internal assessment of strengths and growth areas.

Vision Refinement (Month 2): Review the school's mission and vision statements with the Yayasan Board and senior leadership team. Check that they are still relevant and inspiring. The mission usually stays stable. The 3-5 year vision may be refined to reflect new aspirations or changed circumstances.

Strategic Priorities Identification (Months 2-3): Hold workshops with the Senior Leadership Team, Heads of Faculty and representative teachers. In them, identify 4-6 major strategic priorities for the planning period. These priorities should be the most critical areas for development. They are not a full list of everything the school does. They are the focused initiatives that will drive transformational improvement.

Stakeholder Consultation (Month 3): Present the draft priorities to the Yayasan Board, parent representatives (through Parent Council or focus groups) and student leadership. Gather feedback on relevance, feasibility and fit with community values. In particular, make sure that Indonesian language, Islamic education (where applicable) and local cultural integration get appropriate emphasis.

Goal Setting and Success Metrics (Month 4): For each strategic priority, set specific, measurable goals with clear success indicators. Set baseline data and targets for the end of the strategic planning period, with expected interim milestones.

Resource Mapping (Month 4): Work with the General Manager and Eduversal Finance team to estimate the financial, human and physical resources required for each priority. Make sure this fits long-term financial sustainability and investment capacity.

Approval and Communication (Month 5): Present the complete Strategic Plan to the Yayasan Board for formal approval. Then present it to the full staff, the parent community and (for secondary schools) the student body. Publish an easy-to-read summary that highlights key priorities and what they mean for each stakeholder group.

content.text: Each Multi-Year Strategic Plan must include:

items: Executive Summary (2-3 pages): An overview of the vision, strategic priorities and expected outcomes. It is written for all stakeholders, including parents with limited English proficiency.

School Context and Analysis (5-7 pages): An environmental scan of the school. It includes enrollment trends, academic performance data, Appraisal findings, accreditation status, facilities assessment, staffing profile and competitive positioning. This section shows evidence-based planning. It also gives the baseline for measuring progress.

items.text: Strategic Priorities (15-20 pages): For each of 4-6 priorities, include:
items: Rationale and connection to mission/SLOs
Specific goals with measurable indicators
Major initiatives and action streams
Timeline with key milestones
Resource requirements
Responsibility assignments (Principal, GM, SLT members)
Risk factors and mitigation strategies
Implementation Framework (3-5 pages): How strategic priorities become annual School Improvement Plans. It also covers monitoring processes, reporting schedules and adjustment mechanisms.

Financial Projections (3-5 pages): Multi-year budget implications, capital investment plans, enrollment and revenue projections, and sustainability indicators. These are developed together with the General Manager and Eduversal Finance.

Appendices: Supporting data tables, EASE reports, summaries of stakeholder consultation, and alignment matrices. The matrices show how strategic priorities address Indonesian RKS requirements, Cambridge expectations and CIS/WASC standards.

content.title: Strategic Priority Examples from Partner Schools

content.text: These examples of strategic priorities from across the Eduversal network show the right scope and focus:

items: "Establishing a Culture of Academic Excellence": A secondary school that made better Cambridge examination results its priority. It worked on stronger subject knowledge, assessment literacy, data-driven intervention and university preparation support. Three-year targets included 80% A-C at IGCSE (from a 68% baseline) and university placement partnerships.

"Becoming a Leader in EAL Support": A primary school with 65% EAL (English as an Additional Language) learners. It invested in specialized EAL staffing, differentiated curriculum frameworks, parent language programs and bilingual learning support systems. Goals included all EAL students making expected progress and 90% gaining Cambridge English qualifications suitable for their age.

"Integrating Sustainability Education": An all-through school building environmental sustainability into its curriculum, operations and community engagement. Initiatives included campus greening, student-led sustainability projects, green building certifications, and SDGs (the UN Sustainable Development Goals) in the curriculum (see Section 5: Curriculum Architecture).

"Achieving CIS Accreditation": A mature school preparing for its first CIS/WASC accreditation. It is systematically improving governance, curriculum documentation, assessment systems, professional learning and evidence collection. The five-year pathway included self-study, candidacy and full accreditation.

"Expanding Access Through Boarding Integration": A day school adding Islamic boarding (pesantren) facilities. These serve families who want academic and religious education together. The strategic priority covered curriculum integration, staffing for 24-hour care, facilities development, and keeping quality high while enrollment grows.

content.text: The Multi-Year Strategic Plan meets the Indonesian legal requirements for the Rencana Kerja Sekolah (RKS) in PP No. 57/2021 Pasal 28. It states that education planning is set out in a medium-term work plan (rencana kerja jangka menengah) for a 4 (four) year period. Each year, this plan is broken down into an annual work plan (Pasal 28 ayat (3)-(4)). Some schools run their own strategic cycle over 3 or 5 years. In that case, the RKS mapping they submit to the local education authorities must still cover the 4-year period set by law. The Principal ensures that the strategic plan addresses all eight Indonesian Standard Nasional Pendidikan (National Education Standards):

steps: Graduate Competency Standards (mapped to SLOs (Schoolwide Learner Outcomes) and Profil Pelajar Pancasila competencies)
Content Standards (Cambridge curriculum + Indonesian national subjects)
Process Standards (pedagogical approaches - see Section 7: Teaching Quality)
Assessment Standards (see Section 6: Assessment, Moderation, and Reporting)
Educator and Education Personnel Standards (staffing and professional development)
Facilities and Infrastructure Standards (campus development plans)
Management Standards (governance and operational systems)
Financing Standards (budget and sustainability planning)

content.text: A mapping document in the Strategic Plan appendix shows clear alignment between strategic priorities and SNP requirements. This makes regulatory reporting and inspections by local education authorities easier.

Legal basis: PP No. 57/2021 (Standar Nasional Pendidikan) Pasal 28 ayat (2)-(4). It requires planning to be set out in a medium-term work plan covering four years. An annual work plan gives the details.

content.title: Review and Renewal Cycle
content.text:
The Multi-Year Strategic Plan is formally reviewed each year during School Improvement Plan development (see Section 4.3). The review checks progress toward goals and adjusts initiatives based on implementation experience. Major revision or renewal happens at the end of the 3-5 year cycle. However, significant changes in circumstances may trigger an earlier full review. Examples are major enrollment shifts, leadership transitions, regulatory changes, or changes in the Yayasan's strategic direction.

The Principal works with the General Manager to present annual progress reports on strategic priorities. Reports go to both the Yayasan Board (quarterly briefings, annual full review) and Eduversal leadership (through Appraisal visits and semi-annual Board reporting). This dual accountability keeps local ownership while maintaining network alignment.

The School Improvement Plan (SIP) turns the Multi-Year Strategic Plan into annual priorities that people can act on. It sets specific initiatives, timelines, responsibility assignments and success measures. The Strategic Plan gives direction and vision. The SIP drives day-to-day implementation and operational focus.
An effective SIP is:
content.title: 4.2.2 Annual School Improvement Plan (SIP)

items: Focused: Names 3-5 main improvement priorities for the year. It does not list every school activity. These priorities are the most important areas to develop within the wider strategic framework.

Actionable: Breaks each priority into specific initiatives. Each initiative has clear action steps, named responsibilities, resources and deadlines. Teachers and staff should understand exactly what they need to do to support SIP goals.

Measurable: Defines success with quantitative and qualitative indicators. These include baseline data, interim checkpoints (typically quarterly) and year-end targets. It should be possible to check progress objectively.

Evidence-Based: Comes from analysis of the school's own evidence. This includes student data, EASE evaluation findings, Cambridge examination results, parent and student feedback, staff consultation and the review of the previous year's SIP. It is not based on assumptions or on outside trends that have no link to the school's reality.

Aligned: Clearly connects to the Multi-Year Strategic Plan priorities, Schoolwide Learner Outcomes, Indonesian RKS requirements and Cambridge school improvement frameworks. It shows one connected plan, not separate, unrelated initiatives.
Stakeholder-Informed: Includes input from teachers, parents, students, Yayasan and Eduversal leadership. This gives broad ownership and a realistic view of capacity and priorities.

content.text:
The yearly SIP development cycle starts in March/April (Term 3). It follows this process:

April-May: Data Analysis and Reflection

items: Review how the previous year's SIP was carried out and which goals it achieved
Cambridge checkpoint and examination results
Internal assessment data and progress tracking (see Section 6)
Reading levels, standardized testing, and diagnostic assessments
EAL progression and English language proficiency data
Indonesian national subject examination results
Review Appraisal findings and accreditation progress
Analyze stakeholder feedback from parent surveys, student voice activities, and staff consultation
Look at operational data: enrollment trends, attendance patterns, staff retention, budget performance and facilities use
Get input from Appraisal meetings and Eduversal network benchmarking data

content.text:
May: Priority Identification Workshop

The Principal leads a 2-3 day strategic planning workshop with the Senior Leadership Team and Heads of Faculty to:

items: Identify strengths to celebrate and sustain
Choose 3-5 improvement priorities that align with the Multi-Year Strategic Plan
Keep a balance across these domains: academic quality, student wellbeing, operational effectiveness, community engagement and staff development
Test each priority against criteria: impact on student learning, fit with the strategic plan, feasibility given resources and capacity, stakeholder importance, and readiness to start
Draft initial goals and success measures for each priority

content.text:
June: Initiative Design

For each improvement priority, working groups led by relevant SLT or HOF members develop:

items: Specific initiatives and action plans
Theory of change: how the activities will lead to the desired outcomes
Timeline with key milestones and dependencies
Budget and resource requirements
Responsibility matrix (RACI: Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed)
Professional learning needed to carry out the plan
Communication and change management strategies
Risk assessment and mitigation plans

content.text: Late June: Stakeholder Consultation

items: Present the draft SIP to teaching staff. Ask for feedback on feasibility, resource needs and professional learning needs
Consult the Parent Council on priorities that affect parent partnership and the school community
For secondary schools, ask student leaders for input on priorities that affect student experience
Review with the Yayasan Board to check alignment with Foundation priorities and confirm that resources are available
Share with Eduversal management (through the GM) for network alignment and support planning

content.text: July: Finalization and Approval

items: Add the feedback and finalize the SIP document
Get formal approval from the Yayasan Board
Submit to Eduversal for network coordination and resource allocation
Submit the RKAS (annual activity and budget plan) to local education authorities, as Indonesian regulations require
Publish the SIP and share it with the whole school community. Use staff meetings, parent information sessions and easy-to-read summary documents (Bahasa Indonesia and English)

items: Overview of year's priorities and expected outcomes
Connection to Multi-Year Strategic Plan
Key investments and resource allocations

content.text: The SIP succeeds only when it is the living framework for school operations, not a document filed away after approval. The Principal builds the SIP into school life through:

items: Staff Meeting Focus: Plan weekly staff meetings to include regular SIP progress updates. Use them to celebrate successes, solve problems in carrying out the plan, and share good practices that come from improvement initiatives.

Individual Performance Goals: Align teacher and staff appraisal goals (see Section 7.3: Eduversal Teacher Appraisal System) with SIP priorities. This way, personal professional learning objectives support school-wide improvement.

Budget Decisions: Refer to SIP priorities when you make spending decisions during the year. This keeps spending linked to the strategic focus, so it does not drift toward immediate operational demands.

Professional Learning: Design ongoing professional development (Development of Teaching Proficiency, INSET days, external training) specifically to build the capacity to carry out SIP initiatives. (See Section 7.7: Professional Learning Communities and Section 12.6: Professional Development.)

Student and Parent Communication: Share SIP progress regularly in newsletters, assemblies, parent-teacher conferences and school events. This helps stakeholders understand how improvement initiatives benefit students.
Leadership Team Agenda: Give each SIP priority a standing item on the SLT meeting agenda. This makes sure there is regular monitoring, resource allocation decisions and problem-solving.

content.title: Example SIP Priority: Improving Academic Excellence in Mathematics
content.text:
Here is a sample SIP priority. It shows the level of detail and action expected:

**Priority 2: Strengthening Mathematics Achievement Across Primary School**

**Rationale:** In the 2024 Cambridge Primary Checkpoint results, only 58% of Year 6 students reached the expected standard in Mathematics (compared to 76% in English). Performance was especially weak in problem-solving and reasoning. Internal assessment data shows that the gap starts in Key Stage 1. There is not enough focus on mathematical reasoning and on the concrete-pictorial-abstract progression. Teacher surveys show low confidence in teaching mastery approaches and in supporting diverse learners in mathematics.

**Connection to Strategic Plan:** Aligns with Strategic Priority 1 "Establishing Culture of Academic Excellence". It directly supports SLO 1 (Academic Excellence) and SLO 5 (Innovation through mathematical thinking).

**Goals and Success Measures:**
Quantitative Targets:

items: 75% of Year 6 students achieve expected standard in Mathematics Checkpoint (from 58% baseline)
100% of students make expected progress in Mathematics across the year (minimum 1.0 sublevel improvement)
40% of students exceed expected progress (1.5+ sublevels improvement)
The achievement gap between EAL students and native English speakers falls from 18% to 10%

content.text: Qualitative Targets:

items: All teachers consistently use the CPA approach in mathematics teaching (shown in lesson observations)
80% of teachers report increased confidence teaching mathematical reasoning (end-of-year survey)
Student surveys show 85% agree "I enjoy mathematics lessons" (from 67% baseline)
Learning walks show differentiated support and extension in 90% of mathematics lessons

content.text: Initiative 2.1: Implementing Mathematics Mastery Approach Actions:

items: June-July: 3 teachers attend external White Rose Maths training; develop internal training plan
August: Whole-staff INSET on CPA approach and variation theory in mathematics
Sept-Dec: Introduce new mathematics schemes of work, based on mastery principles, for Years 1-3
Jan-Apr: Extend to Years 4-6 with differentiated pathways
Throughout year: Purchase manipulatives for all classrooms (budget: IDR 45 million)
Ongoing: Weekly mathematics subject leader meeting to improve schemes and share practices

content.text:
Responsibility: Mathematics Subject Leader (lead), Primary Principal (accountable), all primary teachers (responsible for implementation)

Success Indicators:

items: Q1: Schemes of work completed for Years 1-3; manipulatives distributed
Q2: Lesson observations show 70% of teachers using the CPA approach well
Q3: Schemes extended to Years 4-6; teacher confidence survey shows 60% confident
Q4: 85% of teachers consistently use mastery approaches; student progress data shows faster progress

content.text: Initiative 2.2: Differentiated Support and Extension System Actions:

items: August: Analyze Year 2-6 mathematics data to find students who need intervention or extension
September: Set up three intervention groups per year level (15 students total) for targeted support
September: Start an enrichment mathematics club for high-achieving students (30 students)
Ongoing: Progress monitoring every two weeks for intervention students using diagnostic assessments
Nov and March: Review and adjust groupings based on progress data
Throughout: In-class differentiation coaching for all teachers through learning walks and co-planning

content.text:
Responsibility: Learning Support Coordinator (lead interventions), Mathematics Subject Leader (lead extension), Primary Principal (monitor impact)

Resources: 0.4 FTE extra teacher time for intervention groups (IDR 180 million annually)

Success Indicators:

items: Q1: Intervention groups established; enrichment program launched
Q2: 60% of intervention students show faster progress; enrichment students compete in external mathematics challenges
Q3: Gap analysis shows achievement differences getting smaller
Q4: 75% of intervention students reach expected standard; 100% make better than expected progress

content.text: Initiative 2.3: Data-Driven Instruction and Assessment Actions:

items: August: Train all primary teachers to use assessment data to guide teaching
Ongoing: Use a standardized assessment schedule (baseline in Sept, checkpoints in Nov, Feb, May)
Ongoing: The mathematics subject leader analyzes class and school-level data every month and identifies trends
Each term: Faculty data review meetings to look at progress, identify students at risk and adjust teaching
Throughout: Lesson planning clearly refers to assessment data and earlier learning gaps

content.text:
Responsibility: Assessment Coordinator (lead), Mathematics Subject Leader (analyze data), all teachers (responsive instruction)

Success Indicators:

items: Q1: Assessment schedule implemented; baseline data establishes targets for all students
Q2: Teacher planning documents show data use; intervention changes are made based on November checkpoint data
Q3: Data review meetings show consistent analysis and action planning at class level
Q4: The link between formative assessment accuracy and student progress outcomes shows that data is used well

content.text: Monitoring Process:

items: Monthly: Mathematics Subject Leader reports progress to SLT with data and evidence
Quarterly: Deep-dive review of mathematics achievement in SLT meeting; adjust strategies as needed
Termly: Report progress to the Yayasan Board and through Eduversal Supervisi
Annually: Full evaluation of impact and what it means for the next year's SIP

content.text: Budget: IDR 225 million total

items: Manipulatives and resources: IDR 45 million
Extra teaching time for interventions: IDR 180 million
Professional development (external training, resources): Included in school PD budget

content.text: Risk Factors:

items: Teacher turnover breaks continuity (mitigation: document approaches clearly; build capacity across several teachers)
Not enough time for collaboration and planning (mitigation: protect weekly subject leader time; reduce other meeting burdens)
Parent understanding and support for mastery approach (mitigation: parent information sessions; home learning guidance)

content.text: This example shows the level of detail, action and evidence expected for each SIP priority. Teachers who read this part of the SIP understand exactly what is expected, how it will be supported and how success will be measured.

editorialNotes.text: Note on the RKS legal basis. This clause previously anchored RKS to Permendikbud No. 28/2016 - which the manual's own regulation index (Section 20.2) lists as the SPMI/SPME quality-assurance regulation, not the school work-plan rule - and stated no statutory plan period. The anchor was corrected on 2026-08-20 against the salinan of PP No. 57/2021 (Standar Nasional Pendidikan): Pasal 28 ayat (2)-(4) requires planning to be set out in a medium-term work plan covering 4 (four) years, detailed by an annual work plan. PP No. 4/2022 did not amend Pasal 28.

2026-10-02 (Alif): 'bi-weekly' → 'every two weeks' and 'bi-annual' → 'twice-yearly' / 'twice a year' ('annually or bi-annually' → 'once or twice a year'). Both words have two readings (twice a week / every two weeks; twice a year / every two years), which ESL readers cannot resolve; the meaning chosen is the one the context gives (S02's two reports are end of Semester 1 and end of year).

content.text: Strategic planning and school improvement need strong systems to track progress toward goals. Eduversal Partner Schools use a full set of Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). These are monitored through EduNav, our own school management and quality assurance platform, alongside traditional reporting methods.

Our KPI framework balances academic outcomes, operational effectiveness, stakeholder satisfaction and organizational health. It covers six domains that align with our mission and Schoolwide Learner Outcomes.

Domain 1: Academic Excellence and Student Outcomes

These indicators measure the school's core purpose—student learning and achievement:

items: Percentage achieving A-C at IGCSE (target: 75%+ for established programs)
Percentage achieving A-B at A-Level (target: 60%+ for established programs)
Percentage achieving expected standard at Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoints
Value-added scores showing progress from baseline assessments to final examinations
Subject-level performance compared to Cambridge international benchmarks
Trend analysis over a 3-year rolling average, to allow for differences between cohorts
content.title: 4.3.1 KPI Framework and Categories

content.text: Internal Academic Progress

items: Percentage of students making expected progress across the year in core subjects (target: 100%)
Percentage exceeding expected progress (target: 40%+)
Achievement of year-level learning objectives, measured by standardized internal assessments
Reading age progress for primary students (target: minimum 12 months per academic year)
EAL student progress rates compared to native English speakers (target: gap < 10%)
Indonesian national subject performance (Bahasa Indonesia, Pendidikan Agama Islam, PPKN)

content.text: Student Engagement and Wellbeing

items: Attendance rate (target: 95%+)
Student satisfaction survey results (target: 85%+ positive responses)
Participation in co-curricular activities (target: 100% involved in at least one activity)
Behavioral incident rates and trends
Student voice survey results on safety, belonging, and engagement
Destination data and university placement success (secondary schools)

content.text:
Domain 2: Teaching Quality and Professional Practice

Indicators of the quality of teaching and the ongoing improvement of teaching staff (see Section 7: Teaching Quality):

items: Percentage of teaching judged "Good" or "Outstanding" in lesson observations (target: 90%+)
Teacher appraisal completion rate and quality of goal-setting (target: 100%)
Hours of professional learning per teacher (target: 40+ hours a year)
Teacher retention rate (target: 85%+ retention from one year to the next)
How faithfully teachers use key teaching frameworks (mastery learning, differentiation, EAL strategies), as measured through learning walks
Teacher self-efficacy and satisfaction survey results
Quality of curriculum documentation and schemes of work

content.text:
Domain 3: Inclusion and Learning Support

Indicators that show how well the school supports diverse learners (see Section 8: Inclusion, EAL, and Learning Support):

items: Percentage of identified SEN (special educational needs) students making expected progress (target: 100%)
EAL (English as an Additional Language) students moving up through proficiency levels (target: 80% move up at least one level each year)
Quality of how Individual Education Plans (IEPs) and EAL Support Plans are carried out
Parent satisfaction with learning support (target: 90%+ satisfied)
How quickly the school identifies struggling learners and starts intervention
Signs of inclusive practice seen in classroom observations

content.text:
Domain 4: Operational Effectiveness and Compliance

Indicators that show the school runs efficiently and meets regulatory requirements:

items: Enrollment numbers compared with capacity and budget projections
Financial performance against budget (monthly variance reporting)
Staff-to-student ratios by level and subject area
Use of facilities and completion rates for maintenance work
Compliance with Indonesian regulatory requirements (how complete the documentation is, inspection findings)
Cambridge Centre compliance (quality of examination administration, coursework submission rates, inspection outcomes)
Accreditation progress toward CIS/WASC milestones
Health and safety incident rates and audit findings
Uptime of IT systems and use of the digital learning platform

content.text:
Domain 5: Stakeholder Engagement and Satisfaction

Indicators that show how well the school works with families and the community:

items: Parent satisfaction survey results (target: 85%+ satisfied or very satisfied)
Parent-teacher conference participation rate (target: 95%+)
Parent education workshop attendance
Parent communication effectiveness ratings
Student recruitment and enrollment trends (applications, conversion rates, wait lists)
Community partnership activities and outreach
Alumni engagement (for mature schools)

content.text:
Domain 6: Strategic Plan Implementation

Indicators that track progress toward the Multi-Year Strategic Plan and the annual SIP priorities:

items: SIP initiative completion rate (major milestones delivered on time)
Achievement of SIP goal targets (quantitative and qualitative measures)
Budget variance for strategic initiatives (whether spending matches the plans)
EASE assessment ratings
Appraisal evaluations year-over-year improvement
Accreditation preparedness indicators

content.text:
EduNav is the central platform for KPI monitoring, data visualization and evidence management in all Eduversal Partner Schools. It gives real-time dashboards to many users, and each role gets the access and functions it needs.

EduNav: a full school management information system built by PT. Global Zerone Digital for Eduversal. It provides:
content.title: 4.3.2 EduNav Dashboard System

steps: Real-time dashboards and KPI tracking
Evidence repository for accreditation
Student information management
Assessment data integration (including EASE results)
Financial and administrative workflows
Role-based access for students, teachers, staff, parents

content.text: The Principal's main dashboard shows the overall health of the school at a glance:

items: Traffic Light Indicators: Each major KPI category shows a status: green (on target), amber (needs attention) or red (well below target). The status is based on current performance against set benchmarks.
Trend Graphs: Charts of key metrics over time (weekly, monthly, termly, annually). They help leaders see patterns and give early warning when performance is falling.
Alert System: Automatic notifications when a metric falls outside the acceptable range, so the school can act before problems grow.
Drill-Down Capability: Users click from summary indicators to detailed data by year level, class, subject area or individual student. This helps them find the exact problem and target their action.
SIP Progress Tracking: A visual view of the completion status of each SIP initiative, with milestone completion, who is responsible, and timeline management.

Comparative Analytics: Benchmarking against other Eduversal Partner Schools (anonymized) and Cambridge international averages where applicable. This gives context for reading the school's performance.

content.text: Detailed tools for monitoring academic performance include:

items: Student Progress Tracker: A profile for each student. It shows assessment results over time, progress toward learning objectives, intervention history and predictive analytics for examination performance.

Class and Subject Performance: Analysis of achievement by class, subject and teacher. It shows the spread of performance levels, identifies classes or subjects that need extra support and highlights excellent practice.
EAL and SEN Tracking: Special views of English language proficiency progress, SEN student progress against IEP goals, and how well intervention programs work.
Assessment Calendar and Completion: Monitoring of scheduled assessments, completion rates, data entry compliance, and moderation status (see Section 6: Assessment, Moderation, and Reporting).

content.text: Tools for monitoring day-to-day school operations:

items: Attendance Monitoring: Real-time attendance data by class and by individual student. It identifies worrying patterns and sends automatic messages to parents about absences.
Behavioral Tracking: Incident logging, pattern analysis, intervention tracking and records of restorative practice.
Facilities Management: Work order tracking, maintenance scheduling, safety inspection logs, and asset management.
Budget Monitoring: Tracking of spending against the approved budget by cost center, purchase order management and variance reporting.

content.text: Tools for managing parent partnership and community engagement:

items: Communication Log: Records of parent contacts, meeting notes and follow-up actions, so communication stays consistent.
Survey Results: Analysis of parent and student satisfaction surveys, with trends over time and breakdowns by demographic group.
Event Participation: Tracking of parent attendance at school events, workshops, conferences, and volunteer activities.

content.text: Special tools for managing quality assurance and preparing for accreditation:

items: Appraisal Progress: Completion status of self-evaluation in all domains, status of evidence collection, and tracking of action plans for areas that need improvement.

Evidence Repository: One central place to store and tag the documents that support accreditation standards. These include policies, meeting minutes, student work samples, observation reports, survey results, professional learning records and other documents required for the CIS/WASC self-study.
Standards Alignment Matrix: A visual map showing how school practices and evidence address specific CIS/WASC standards and Indonesian SNP requirements. It identifies gaps that need attention.

Accreditation Milestone Tracker: Timeline and completion status for major accreditation activities: self-study chapters, stakeholder surveys, visiting team preparation and carrying out the action plan.

content.text: Tools for monitoring and supporting teacher development (see Section 7.7: Professional Learning Communities and Section 12.6: Professional Development):

items: Professional Learning Hours: Tracking each teacher's participation against annual targets. This covers formal professional development, Development of Teaching Proficiency, collaborative planning and self-directed learning.

Appraisal Cycle Management: Timeline tracking for appraisal observations, goal-setting meetings, mid-year reviews and final evaluations. This makes sure the school meets Eduversal Appraisal Program requirements.
Observation Data: Combined lesson observation findings that show school-wide strengths and development needs. These findings shape professional learning priorities.
Qualification and Certification Tracking: Monitoring of teacher credentials, Cambridge training completion, safeguarding certifications, and renewal requirements.

content.text: EduNav's value depends on accurate data that is entered on time. The Principal sets clear protocols:

items: Responsibility Matrix: A clear assignment of data entry duties. Teachers are responsible for formative assessments and attendance, and subject leaders for moderation outcomes. Administrative staff are responsible for enrollment and operational data, and SLT for strategic indicators.
Quality Assurance Procedures: Regular checks of data accuracy, verification before data is used for decisions, and a process to correct errors when they are found.
Training and Support: Ongoing professional learning for staff on correct data entry, on data definitions and standards, and on using EduNav tools to improve teaching.
Compliance Monitoring: Dashboard indicators show data entry completion rates and timeliness. There is follow-up on incomplete or late submissions, so the system stays up to date.

content.text: Good KPI targets are ambitious but realistic. They draw on several data sources:
content.title: 4.3.3 KPI Target-Setting and Review

items: Historical Performance: A three-year trend analysis sets the baseline and shows realistic paths for improvement. It takes account of differences between cohorts and other context factors.

Network Benchmarking: Comparison with similar Eduversal Partner Schools gives context for suitable target levels. It considers factors such as school maturity, student demographics and resource levels.
Cambridge International Standards: Where available, Cambridge international benchmarking data helps set realistic expectations for examination performance and checkpoint achievement.
Strategic Plan Alignment: Targets link directly to the Multi-Year Strategic Plan goals. This makes annual KPIs steps toward the longer-term vision, not unconnected metrics.
Capacity Assessment: An honest review of current staffing, resources, professional learning needs and organizational readiness. It shows what improvement is possible within the annual cycle.

Stakeholder Input: The school consults the Yayasan Board, Eduversal leadership (through the GM) and staff. This makes targets reflect shared expectations and commitment, not top-down orders that are likely to cause resistance.

content.text: Not all students, classes or subgroups face the same expectations. The Principal sets differentiated targets. These keep expectations high while taking account of each starting point:

items: Individual Student Progress Targets: Each student has personal progress targets, not one standard for everyone. These are based on baseline assessments, prior achievement and EAL/SEN factors. They include minimum expected progress and stretch goals for high achievers.

Year Group Targets: These reflect the features of each cohort. A Year 7 cohort that enters well below expected levels has different one-year achievement targets from a cohort that enters at the standard level. Multi-year goals still aim to bring them together.

Subject-Specific Targets: New or developing subjects (recently introduced sciences, growing language programs) may have development-phase targets that differ from those of established, mature curriculum areas.

Staged Implementation Targets: When the school introduces new initiatives (EAL framework, mastery mathematics, restorative behavior approaches), targets rise across the implementation phases. The pilot year focuses on implementation fidelity. Later years focus on achieving outcomes.

content.title: Two kinds of review
content.text: KPIs are reviewed quarterly — four times a year. The academic calendar sets the dates, not the EASE Weeks. The four reviews are still not the same exercise, because different assessment data is available at each point of the year. EASE Weeks 1 and 3 fall mid-semester and produce EASE Growth results. These cover reasoning and literacy, are independent of the curriculum and carry no report-card weight. EASE Weeks 2 and 4 fall at semester-end and produce Synchronized Test results. These cover subject content and count toward the student's grade. The review cycle follows that difference.

content.title: Interim check-ins (Quarters 1 and 3)
content.text: An interim check-in looks only at the EASE Growth data from that week. This is the trend in Mathematical Reasoning, Science Literacy and English Reading. It is an early signal, not a decision point.

items: No formal red / amber / green KPI status is given. The dashboard status from the previous full review stays until the next one.
Findings are not reported to the Yayasan Board. The check-in is internal monitoring by the Senior Leadership Team and the Principal.

Grades 4-6 take EASE Growth once a year, in Semester 2, so they have no Growth data at the Quarter 1 check-in. Record "no data this cycle; assessed at the next full review". This is the expected pattern for those grades, not a gap to escalate.
Where the trend is falling, the response is an adjustment to teaching or support inside the department. It is not a KPI re-rating.

content.title: Full reviews (Quarters 2 and 4)
content.text: A full review assesses all six KPI domains: Academic Excellence, Teaching Quality, Inclusion, Operational, Stakeholder Engagement, and Strategic Plan Implementation. It uses the Synchronized Test results together with the other end-of-semester indicators (attendance, behavior, engagement, SIP implementation evidence, stakeholder feedback).

items: The formal red / amber / green status is assigned here, for every domain.
Results are reported to the Yayasan Board and feed the quarterly Board meeting (see 4.8.2 Governance Reporting).
Quarter 2 also reviews progress toward annual targets: on track, at risk, or exceeding. It reallocates resources where a target is at risk and a semester is still to run.
Quarter 4 is the summative review. It covers achievement against all annual KPI targets, the evaluation of SIP delivery, and the evidence for setting next year's targets.

content.text: Each quarterly review produces:

items: KPI Dashboard Report: A report from EduNav that shows the current status of all indicators, with trend analysis and variance from targets.

Narrative Analysis: The Principal's written explanation of the data. It answers: What does the data tell us? Why are we seeing these patterns? What actions does the data point to? How confident are we in the data quality and our interpretation?
Action Plans: Specific changes that come out of the review — adjustments to SIP implementation, resource reallocations, changes to interventions, or professional learning needs.

Stakeholder Communication: Suitable summaries for each audience. SLT and the Yayasan Board get detailed analysis. Teaching staff and parents get easy-to-read highlights. Eduversal Supervisi gets a strategic overview.

content.text: KPIs help school improvement only when they actively shape decisions, rather than sitting as compliance documents. The Principal builds data literacy and a culture of inquiry across the school.

Structured protocols guide teams when they analyze data together:

Teaching Team Data Meetings (monthly, by Faculty or Department):
content.title: 4.3.4 Data-Driven Decision Making

steps: Review the agreed focus data (recent assessments, progress tracking, formative evidence)
Identify patterns: what is working well, what is worrying, what is surprising
Suggest possible causes, using professional knowledge and understanding of the context
Plan teaching responses: changes to differentiation, intervention strategies, ways to re-teach
Assign responsibility and timeline for actions
Schedule a follow-up to check the impact of the changes

content.text: SLT Data Deep Dives (quarterly, in line with KPI reviews):

steps: Choose 2-3 priority KPIs for deep analysis, based on current performance or strategic importance
Look at several data sources and points of view to cross-check understanding
Carry out root cause analysis to find the system-level factors behind the outcomes
Explore possible solutions that have evidence of working, from research and network practice
Make resource allocation, policy, or initiative design decisions
Communicate decisions openly, with the reasons and the success criteria

content.text: Individual Student Case Reviews (ongoing as needed):

steps: Bring together the staff involved (class teacher, subject teachers, learning support, pastoral care)
Review the student's full profile: academic progress, attendance, behavior, wellbeing and family context
Analyze how well the current support works and find the gaps
Write or revise the Individual Education Plan or intervention strategy
Name a case coordinator and set a monitoring schedule
Share the plan with parents, and involve the student in setting goals where appropriate

content.text: Many teachers arrive with little training in data analysis and evidence-based practice. The Principal invests in building teachers' data literacy:

items: Understanding Assessment Data: Professional learning on how to read standardized assessment results and how to use formative assessment well. It also covers how to tell real signals from noise in classroom data (see Section 6: Assessment, Moderation, and Reporting).

Progress Measurement: Training on tracking each student's growth over time and calculating value-added measures. It also covers the difference between progress and attainment, and how to set suitable progress targets.
Data Visualization: Building skills to present data clearly in graphs, charts and dashboards. These make patterns easy to see and understand for non-technical audiences, including parents.

Inquiry Mindset: Developing professional habits: curiosity about student learning, willingness to question assumptions, and comfort with ambiguity and complexity. It also means a commitment to practice based on evidence, not on intuition.

Ethical Data Use: Understanding privacy issues, and not using data to label students in harmful ways or to lower expectations of them. Recognizing the limits and biases of assessment, and keeping the focus on using data to help students, not to judge them.

content.text: The Principal promotes data-driven practice but guards against these common pitfalls:

items: Teaching to the Test: Data is used to understand what students need to learn. It is not used to narrow the curriculum to tested content, or to put test preparation before real learning.
Reductionism: Remembering that students are complex human beings, not numbers. Important outcomes are not always easy to measure, and quantitative data need qualitative interpretation.

Analysis Paralysis: Balancing careful analysis with timely action. Perfect understanding is impossible. A reasonable decision based on the best evidence available is better than delaying intervention while waiting for more data.

Blame and Shame: Building a culture where data show chances to improve, not reasons to blame teachers, students or families. Data meetings focus on solving professional problems, not on enforcing accountability.

Dashboard Obsession: Not relying too much on EduNav dashboards. Direct classroom observation, conversations with students, teachers' professional judgment and qualitative evidence give essential context for reading the numbers.

content.text: KPIs give important numerical indicators. But full school improvement needs several kinds of evidence:

items: Qualitative Observations: Regular learning walks, lesson observations and classroom visits by the Principal and SLT. These give descriptive evidence of teaching quality, student engagement and the learning environment that numbers do not capture.

Student Work Analysis: A regular, planned review of student work samples across classes and subjects. It shows depth of understanding, quality of thinking, how well feedback works, and how faithfully the curriculum is delivered.

Stakeholder Voice: Student focus groups, parent interviews, staff consultation and community feedback. These give views on school climate, how well programs work, and improvement priorities that surveys alone cannot capture.
Documentary Evidence: Review of planning documents, meeting minutes, records of how policies are put into practice, and other records. These show how the organization works and whether it complies.
Comparative Case Studies: A detailed look at individual students' learning journeys or at specific programs in action. These give a rich story that adds to the statistical patterns.

content.text: The Principal makes sure that SLT meetings, faculty data reviews and SIP monitoring combine quantitative KPI data with these qualitative sources. This gives a complete picture that supports sound decisions.

editorialNotes.title: Note on this cycle
editorialNotes.text: Revised 2026-08-17. The cycle previously ran four equivalent reviews, each tied to one of four administrations of a single subject-based EASE exam. Under the AY 2026-2027 model the four EASE Weeks do different things, so two of the four reviews no longer have subject-attainment data to assess. Rather than ask them to rate KPI domains on a curriculum-independent reasoning benchmark, the cycle now distinguishes interim check-ins from full reviews. Decided by the Academic Board, 2026-08-17. Review dates follow the academic calendar; Quarter 4 moved from June/July to May/June because the academic year closes in June. (Revised 2026-08-20: an earlier version scheduled the reviews to follow the four EASE Weeks and tied the review dates to them. The reviews are quarterly calendar events — the EASE Weeks supply data to them but do not set their dates.)

content.text: Regular, planned monitoring and evaluation turn strategic plans from hopes into action. They check that initiatives run as designed. They also keep progress toward goals under regular review, so the school can make adjustments in time.

Eduversal's Appraisal Program gives Partner Schools full external evaluation and support for improvement. It works through an annual appraisal cycle. Eduversal Subject Specialist teams carry it out against the Eduversal School Appraisal Framework (see Section 17.8 for the full process). The cycle has two purposes: quality assurance, which upholds network standards, and capacity building, which supports Principal and teacher development.
The Appraisal Program has two connected evaluation systems:

items: Purpose: Evaluate how the school performs as an institution across the five domains (33 aspects) of the Eduversal School Appraisal Framework

Cycle: Two on-site visits per academic year: Phase 1 (Teaching Quality Visit) and Phase 3 (Validation Visit). There are also three online stages. A Phase 0 Kickoff comes before Phase 1, and a Phase 2 Progress Check-in comes between the visits. A Phase 4 Impact Review takes place near the end of the academic year
Conducted by: Eduversal Subject Specialist teams. Each visit has five specialists, one per domain, and always includes one of the school's Visit Supervisors
Five Evaluation Domains:
content.title: 4.4.1 Appraisal Program

steps: D1 - Leadership & Governance: vision and strategic direction, SMART goals, leadership structure, performance management, governance and compliance

D2 - Teaching & Learning Quality: lesson planning and observation records, assessment methods, student goal-setting, feedback quality, evaluation of teaching, LMS (learning management system) and technology integration

D3 - Curriculum & Academic Programs: subject department structure, department meetings and HoD coordination, formal observations and walkthroughs, mentoring and peer observation, PD evaluation, resources, digital policy

D4 - Student Achievement & Learning Outcomes: achievement data and dashboards, the Olympiad program and its wellbeing management, support for advanced students, language support, support for extra learning needs

D5 - School Culture & Community: culture, climate and student behavior, safeguarding and child protection, communication structures, co-curricular programs, parent and community engagement, staff wellbeing

content.text: 2. Teacher Appraisal

items: Purpose: Assess each teacher's performance and support their professional growth

Frequency: Ongoing throughout the year. The school's own appraisers make at least three formal observations per semester and record them in Edunav. The End-of-Year Conference takes place in Semester 2

Conducted by: The school's own appraisers (Subject Leader / Head of Department, Principal, or Academic / Cambridge Coordinator). Observations by Eduversal Subject Specialists during visits are formative only. They never produce or change a teacher's F2 score
Planning and Organization (lesson planning, resource preparation)
Classroom Management (learning environment, student behavior management)
Instruction (teaching strategies, student engagement, differentiation)
Assessment (formative/summative practices, feedback quality)
Administrative documentation review
Student satisfaction surveys
Teacher's work inspection (professionalism, collaboration)
Post-observation conferences and development planning

content.text: The School Appraisal runs as a Phase 0-4 cycle across the academic year. Phases 0-3 are completed within Semester 1. The Phase 4 Impact Review takes place near the end of the year. It reviews the two School Development Priorities and creates no new Domain Rating. Section 17.8 describes each phase in full:

steps: Phase 0 - Kickoff (online, about three weeks before the Phase 1 visit): the school receives self-evaluation instructions and the School Appraisal: Evidence Guide 26-27. The school rates itself on the 33 aspects of the five domains and links evidence to each aspect. It completes or updates the Self-Evaluation Summary and the working evidence links in the Evidence Guide. This is mandatory at least five working days before each on-site visit. The visit cannot go ahead without it.

Phase 1 - Teaching Quality Visit (on-site, 1-2 days): five Subject Specialists visit, one per domain. They focus on classroom practice, teacher observation, curriculum implementation and assessment quality. The visit includes formative lesson observations (no teacher scores), quick random classroom walkthroughs and feedback sessions with the observed teachers. It also includes interviews with students, teachers and school management.

Phase 2 - Progress Check-in (online, 1-2 hours): the school's Visit I Supervisor leads it at the midpoint between the two visits. It covers self-appraisal progress across the five domains, progress on the action plan, and new concerns.

Phase 3 - Leadership, Technology & Facility Visit, the 'Validation Visit' (on-site, 1-2 days, 55-63 days after Phase 1): a five-person team validates the school's self-appraisal. It does this through leadership and coordinator meetings, teacher and student focus groups, a review of facilities and operational systems, and spot-check walkthroughs. The team then produces the Annual School Quality Report. Each on-site visit ends with an oral exit report to the Principal and leadership team.

content.text: The school keeps its Self-Evaluation evidence in its own online storage. It links the evidence, aspect by aspect, in the School Appraisal: Evidence Guide 26-27 workbook. The school sends this workbook to its Visit I Supervisor. The evidence includes:

items: Strategic plan and School Improvement Plan (SIP) with progress updates
School organizational chart and leadership structure
Professional development records and teacher qualifications
Student performance data (EASE results, Cambridge examinations, internal assessments)
Curriculum documentation and assessment samples
Meeting minutes, policies, and governance records
Evidence organized by the five domains and 33 aspects of the School Appraisal Framework

content.text:
The appraisal cycle produces these deliverables:

1. Annual School Quality Report (within 3 weeks of the Phase 3 Validation Visit). It goes to the Eduversal Chief Academic Officer (CAO), the School Principal and the Academic Coordinator.

items: A rating for each of the five domains on the 1-4 scale, with specific commendations (minimum 2) and priority recommendations (maximum 3)

A Development Rating for each domain, in four bands: Outstanding (3.5-4.0) / Strong (2.5-3.4) / Developing (1.5-2.4) / Needs Intervention (1.0-1.4). The rating is a development indicator, not a ranking. Eduversal does not publish a single composite school score

School-level, anonymized Teacher Appraisal aggregate data and the EASE Academic participation rate. Also the school's EASE Assessment performance summary and the EASE Growth Version 1 baseline summary, as context only (not scored)

content.text: 2. Formative Observation Feedback (no scores)

items: Formative feedback (Glow / Grow / Go) goes directly to each observed teacher. Visit observations carry no scores and no weight in any teacher's appraisal. The official classroom-observation score comes solely from the school's own appraisers

A Domain-2 validation memo to the school. It says whether the visit evidence supports the school's own observation ratings, and explains the gap where it does not. The visiting team never issues or retrospectively changes individual teacher scores
Development recommendations and resources
Professional learning priorities

content.text: 3. School Development Plan (Appraisal Suite: School Development Plan 26-27) for the two School Development Priorities agreed in the report

items: How recommendations will be addressed
Responsibility assignments and timelines
Success criteria and monitoring approach
Resources needed for implementation

content.text: 4. EduNav System Updates

items: Appraisal findings logged in EduNav
Connected to relevant KPIs and SIP priorities
Evidence repository updated
Tracking system activated for follow-through

content.text: Within two weeks of receiving the Appraisal Report, the Principal:

steps: Reviews with Leadership: Meets with the Senior Leadership Team to analyze the findings. Together they identify specific actions and who is responsible for each

Develops Action Plan: Moves the two School Development Priorities agreed in the Annual School Quality Report into the School Development Plan. Each priority has owners, realistic timelines and evidence of success

Communicates to Staff: Shares relevant findings with teaching staff: commendations that celebrate strengths, and priorities that need everyone's effort. Personnel matters and sensitive governance matters stay confidential
Integrates into SIP: Adds the required actions to the ongoing School Improvement Plan work and to meeting agendas
Updates Tracking System: Records progress on Appraisal recommendations in EduNav
Schedules Check-ins: Sets up a mid-year review with the GM and/or Eduversal leadership to report progress and deal with obstacles to implementation

content.text: Formal Appraisal visits run on the two-visit cycle (Phase 1 and Phase 3). Ongoing quality monitoring also continues through:

items: Monthly Progress Updates: The Principal sends the GM short progress reports on SIP implementation and the Appraisal action plan
EASE Analysis: review of student assessment results at each EASE Week, used to adjust teaching
Internal School-Based Appraisals: Ongoing lesson observations and teacher appraisals by school leadership (HODs, Principal), using the same frameworks
EduNav Dashboard Monitoring: Real-time tracking of KPIs and school performance indicators
Mid-Year Review: The GM carries out a full progress review (usually February/March). It checks progress on putting the Appraisal recommendations into practice

content.text: Eduversal keeps Appraisal processes consistent and of high quality through:

items: Standardized Protocols: The same observation tools, rubrics and evidence frameworks in all Partner Schools
Appraiser Training: Regular professional development for QMS Team members on evaluation methods and feedback practices
Inter-Rater Reliability: Norming sessions among appraisers, so that they apply the standards consistently
Documentation of Best Practices: A collection of excellent practices found in schools, shared across the network
Feedback Mechanisms: Principals give feedback on how useful the Appraisal is and suggest improvements
Annual Program Review: An evaluation of how well the Appraisal Program drives school improvement

content.text: Between annual Appraisal visits, the Principal sets up internal monitoring. This keeps continuous attention on SIP implementation and finds concerns early.

SLT meetings (usually weekly) include standing agenda items for regular monitoring:

SIP Priority Updates (rotating focus):
content.title: 4.4.2 Internal Monitoring Systems

items: Each meeting looks at 1-2 SIP priorities in depth
The responsible SLT member presents progress on implementation, recent data, successes and challenges
The team solves problems with obstacles and makes decisions about resources
Updates action plans and timelines to match the current situation
Records decisions and shares them with the staff involved

content.text: Data Review:

items: Review of recent assessment results (EASE exams, Cambridge checkpoints, internal assessments)
Analysis of attendance patterns, behavioral data, and student wellbeing indicators
Finding worrying trends or patterns that need intervention
Celebrating good results and practices that work
Assigning follow-up investigations or actions

content.text: Operational Monitoring:

items: Budget performance tracking and variance analysis
Enrollment trends and admissions pipeline
Facilities maintenance and development projects
Staffing concerns and HR matters
Compliance requirements and regulatory deadlines

content.text:
The Principal carries out regular informal learning walks and formal lesson observations as monitoring tools (see Section 7.4: Observation and Feedback Process):

Focus Areas:

items: Learning walks focus on specific SIP priorities. Examples are the new mathematics mastery approach, differentiation for EAL (English as an Additional Language) learners, and good questioning techniques
Allow regular, planned monitoring of changes in teaching practice that are linked to improvement initiatives

content.text: Pattern Analysis:

items: Regular visits show how new practices are being used across the whole school
Whether new practices are used consistently across classrooms
Common challenges requiring extra support
Emerging effective practices worth scaling
Areas needing extra professional learning

content.text: Teacher Feedback and Coaching:

items: Short observation notes and coaching conversations
Links between school improvement priorities and each teacher's practice
Identification of professional learning needs
Support for carrying out Appraisal recommendations

content.text: Documentation:

items: Observation notes recorded in EduNav, which build an evidence trail
Tracking how teaching quality changes over time
Data informing professional development planning

content.text: Curriculum leaders (Heads of Faculty and Subject Coordinators) report to the Principal every month on:

items: Subject Area Progress: How much of the curriculum is covered, which assessments are complete, and trends in student performance
SIP Initiative Implementation: Progress on the improvement actions for each subject
Professional Learning: PD (professional development) activities in the department and what teachers need to develop
Resource Requirements: Materials, technology, or support needed
Concerns and Successes: Issues that need the Principal's attention, and good practices to celebrate

content.text: EASE Monitoring — the four EASE Weeks give the school four planned points when assessment data enters the monitoring cycle. Two EASE Weeks carry EASE Growth and two carry the Synchronized Test, so they answer different questions. See 6.4 for the calendar and 6.14 for the program structure.
EASE Week 1 — Semester 1, mid-semester (EASE Growth):

steps: A first (baseline) reading of reasoning and literacy for the year, Grades 7-12
Finds students whose thinking skills need support early, before their subject grades show the problem
Sets each student's Version 1 baseline in reasoning and literacy
Grades 4-6 do not take EASE Growth this semester. They take it once a year, in Semester 2

content.text: EASE Week 2 — Semester 1, semester-end (Synchronized Test):

steps: Network-wide assessment of subject attainment at the end of Semester 1
Checks how well interventions worked for students identified earlier in the semester
Teaching strategies are adjusted before Semester 2
Feeds into reports to parents and into the planning cycle during the semester break

content.text: EASE Week 3 — Semester 2, mid-semester (EASE Growth):

steps: Second Growth sitting for Grades 7-12. In 2026-27 (Version 1), results are reported as a baseline. Formal comparison with the Semester 1 sitting begins in Phase 2

Grades 4-6 are not part of EASE Week 3. They take their annual Growth test at the start of Semester 2, in a separate window outside the EASE Weeks. In Version 1, every Primary result is treated as baseline evidence
Shows where reasoning or literacy is holding back attainment before the Cambridge external examinations

content.text: EASE Week 4 — Semester 2, semester-end (Synchronized Test):

steps: Network-wide assessment of subject attainment at the end of the year
A full review of the year's progress against targets
Data that guides promotion decisions and holiday intervention
The basis for building the next academic year's SIP and for class placement

content.text:
The school uses regular methods to collect stakeholder feedback as monitoring data:

Student Engagement:

items: Student Council Meetings: Monthly discussions with student representatives about school climate, how well programs work, concerns and suggestions
Student Satisfaction Surveys: Carried out as part of the Teacher Appraisal process. They give feedback on teaching quality and the learning experience
Class Representative Check-ins: Regular informal conversations with class representatives
Suggestion Systems: Anonymous ways to give feedback (physical and digital)

content.text: Parent Partnership:

items: Parent Coffee Mornings: Informal meetings once a term where the Principal hears parents' views
Parent Council Consultations: Regular meetings with elected parent representatives
Parent Satisfaction Surveys: Full yearly surveys on school quality
Individual Parent Feedback: Ongoing contact through conferences, emails and informal conversations

content.text:
The Principal keeps personal routines so that priorities get regular, planned attention:

Weekly Practices:

items: Monday Dashboard Review: Look at the EduNav KPIs, find indicators that need attention, and adjust the week's priorities
Classroom Visibility: The minimum target is to visit every classroom at least once a week for a short walkthrough observation
Staff Pulse Check: Informal conversations with teachers and staff to understand morale, problems in putting plans into practice, and support needs

content.text: Monthly Practices:

items: Deep Dive Analysis: Choose one KPI or SIP priority and examine it closely. This includes data analysis, evidence review and stakeholder consultation
Department Meetings: Attend faculty meetings to see how well teachers work together and how healthy the department is
Financial Review: Review budget performance with the GM and change allocations where needed

content.text: Quarterly Practices:

items: Comprehensive Data Review: Analyze all KPIs to prepare for reporting to the GM and for planning adjustments
SIP Progress Assessment: Check progress against quarterly milestones and make strategic adjustments
Self-Reflection: An honest look at how well the Principal leads and at the strategic direction, before Appraisal follow-up reviews

content.text: Annual Practices:

items: 360-Degree Feedback: Ask for structured feedback on how well the Principal leads from the Yayasan Board, GM, SLT, teaching staff and parent representatives
Professional Goal Setting: Set personal professional learning goals that match school needs and leadership development
Succession Planning: Build leadership skills in staff so that the school has continuity

content.text: Monitoring has value only when its findings lead to action. The Principal sets clear procedures for making changes when monitoring shows problems or opportunities.
Some findings start an automatic review and a possible adjustment:
content.title: 4.4.3 Adjustment and Course Correction

items: Red KPIs: Any indicator that falls significantly below target requires immediate analysis and an action plan within one week
Negative Trends: Three data points in a row that show a decline require investigation, even if overall performance is still acceptable. Early intervention prevents crises
EASE Exam Concerns: If student performance is significantly below expectations, this starts an immediate review of curriculum and teaching
Appraisal Recommendations: Priority actions from the annual Appraisal must be addressed within the set timelines, with progress documented
Repeated Stakeholder Concerns: When several channels (parent feedback, student voice, staff consultation) raise the same issue, it demands serious attention, whatever the objective data shows

Implementation Fidelity Issues: If evidence shows that SIP initiatives are not being carried out as designed, this requires immediate intervention. The school cannot judge whether an initiative works unless it is carried out properly

content.text: When monitoring shows a need for change:

steps: Diagnosis: Carry out a full root cause analysis. Look at the underlying factors, not just the symptoms. Bring together the relevant stakeholders (SLT, affected teachers, curriculum leaders) to make sense of the findings together
Options Generation: List several possible responses, from small adjustments to a complete redesign. For each option, consider resources, timeline, staff capacity and possible impact
Decision-Making: Use the analysis and the options to decide on a specific adjustment. State a clear reason, the expected outcomes and the success criteria
Communication: Explain the changes openly to the stakeholders they affect. Present adjustments as a sign of responsive leadership and commitment to success, not as an admission of failure
Implementation Support: Carry out the adjustment with clear responsibilities, timelines, professional learning support and monitoring of how well it works
Meta-Learning: Think about what the need for an adjustment shows about planning processes, implementation support or monitoring systems. This is a chance for the organization to learn

content.text:
Good monitoring requires judgment about when to keep going despite challenges and when to change direction:

Persist When:

items: Implementation is early and not enough time has passed to expect results
Evidence points to problems in carrying out the plan as designed, not to basic problems with the strategy
Short-term challenges were expected in the original plan
Stakeholders are still committed and see progress, even if the goals are not yet fully achieved
Research and network evidence support the approach despite local obstacles
Appraisal recommendations need steady effort over several years

content.text: Pivot When:

items: The plan is carried out as designed but brings no improvement, or brings unexpected negative effects
The school's situation has changed so much that the original strategy no longer works
Better alternatives appear from new evidence, EASE data or Appraisal findings
Stakeholder resistance is deep, not the usual challenge of managing change
Limited resources make the current approach impossible to sustain

content.text: All significant SIP adjustments are recorded in EduNav, including:

items: What changed and why (evidence basis)
Expected impact on goals and timelines
Resource implications
Communication to stakeholders
Success criteria for adjusted approach
Connection to Appraisal recommendations if relevant

content.text: This record is used for: accountability for decisions, organizational learning, accreditation evidence of a responsive improvement culture, and continuity when leaders change.

editorialNotes.text: Formative feedback (Glow / Grow / Go) delivered directly to each observed teacher — visit observations carry no scores and no weight in any teacher's appraisal (teacher-observation-ownership decision, 2026-08-17: the official classroom-observation score comes solely from the school's own appraisers)

block.text: Note: an earlier version of this madde described a retired appraisal instrument - a single annual multi-day visit by an external quality team, with differently named domains and a different four-label rating scale. That instrument was replaced by the Eduversal School Appraisal Framework described above; Section 17.8 carries the full current process.

content.text: Strategic planning and improvement succeed only when stakeholders are truly involved. Stakeholders are staff, parents, students, the Yayasan and the wider school community. The Principal leads this involvement. It goes beyond token consultation to real participation in choosing priorities, carrying out initiatives and evaluating impact.
Teachers and staff are the main people who carry out school improvement initiatives. Their engagement decides whether strategic priorities turn into changed practice and better student outcomes.

items: Bottom-Up Input: SIP development gives all staff structured chances to share ideas from their classroom experience and professional knowledge. Faculty meetings, anonymous surveys and small group discussions make sure that people beyond the SLT influence priorities.

Voluntary Leadership Opportunities: Improvement initiatives need champions. The Principal invites teachers to lead working groups, pilot new approaches or carry out action research linked to SIP priorities. This gives teachers agency and chances for professional growth.

Transparent Decision-Making: When staff input shapes planning, the Principal clearly acknowledges their contributions. When a suggestion cannot be used, the Principal explains the limits or the reasons. This keeps trust and continued engagement.

Resource Allocation Voice: Teachers take part in budget decisions that affect their work. These include choosing curriculum materials, setting professional learning priorities and designing classroom resources. This increases their commitment to using resources well.
content.title: 4.5.1 Staff Engagement and Ownership

content.text: Ownership needs more than involvement in planning. Staff need support to carry out improvement initiatives successfully:

items: Protected Time: SIP priorities get dedicated time. This comes from Collaborative Planning Time, INSET days, fewer meetings on other matters, and curriculum time that reflects the strategic focus. See Section 7.7: Professional Learning Communities and Section 12.6: Professional Development.
